- **The One and the Many:** The philosopher-priests taught that a single hidden divine entity, symbolized by the sun, was unknowable and transcendent. The infinite Many were parts of this ineffable One.
- **Akhenaten's monotheism:** His short-lived worship of the sun god Aten introduced the idea of oneness, which the priests could not dismiss and had to reconcile with the plurality of the older pantheon.

The article does not say how long Plato spent in Egypt. It also doesn't name a specific teacher. It says he "traveled to Egypt with Euripides to meet with Egyptian philosopher-priests," and that during his stay he became very ill and was cured by a priest using a seawater concoction.

Damien does not name specific Egyptian ideas behind the theory of Forms. He says only that "it was in Egypt that Plato was exposed to many new ideas from the philosopher-priests which in turn formed the nucleus of what would become his philosophy and his theory of Forms." When Xenon asks how exactly these priests influenced Plato, Damien sighs and says it is "one of the most important but least asked questions," and the conversation moves on without a specific answer.

The article does mention other Egyptian contributions Plato reportedly learned about or credited to Egypt, though it does not tie them to the Forms:
- The water clock, which Plato reportedly brought back to Greece.
- Numbers and letters, which Plato attributed to the Egyptian god Theuth in the *Phaedrus*.
